pages.h1: Work gloves: types, ratings & how to choose.
pages.metaTitle: Work Gloves Guide: Types, EN 388 Ratings & Choosing | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to choose work gloves — coated grip vs cut-resistant vs winter-lined, what the EN 388 digits mean, sizing that actually matters, and when a glove is worn out.
pages.lede: The wrong glove doesn't just wear out fast — it gets taken off, and a glove in a pocket protects nothing. Choosing well means matching the coating, the cut level and the fit to the actual task. This hub covers the types and the decision; the EN 388 guide decodes the ratings.

blocks.h2: Match the glove to the hazard, not the job title
blocks.html:
Glove choice starts with one question: what actually threatens the hand? Abrasion from block and brick, cuts from sheet metal or glass, cold from a winter scaffold, oil killing your grip — each points to a different glove, and the ratings system that sorts them is EN 388, the standard for mechanical risks.

The second question is comfort, and it isn't soft: studies of hand injuries keep finding the same thing — gloves that are clumsy, sweaty or badly sized get removed, and the injury happens bare-handed. A slightly less protective glove that stays on beats a bulletproof one in a back pocket.

That's why the modern default for general site work is a thin coated glove — a knitted liner dipped in nitrile or polyurethane — rather than the old leather rigger: near-bare-hand dexterity, real abrasion numbers, and cheap enough to replace the moment it's torn.

blocks.lead: Coating and liner decide what a glove is for. These five families cover the overwhelming majority of tasks.

items.area: PU or nitrile dip · EN 388 rated
items.p: The everyday site glove — dexterity, abrasion resistance and grip, dry or lightly oily. Buy by the box.

items.area: Cut level B–F · steel, glass, blades
items.p: HPPE or steel-fibre liners under the same coatings. Pick the cut letter to the hazard — the EN 388 guide shows how.

items.area: EN 511 cold rating · fleece or acrylic liner
items.p: Cold, numb hands drop things. Lined and often water-repellent for outdoor winter work.
Cleaning, concrete additives, fuels — a different standard (EN ISO 374) and a different glove entirely.
Catering, healthcare, paint prep, inspection. Protection for the product as much as the hand.
Heavy hauling, hot works and welding sit outside the thin-coated world — leather and heat-rated kit still earn their place.

faq.q: What do the numbers on work gloves mean?
faq.a: They're the EN 388 rating for mechanical risks: four digits for abrasion, cut (coup test), tear and puncture, then optionally a letter A–F for the ISO 13997 cut test and a P for impact protection. Higher is better in each position; X means untested.

faq.q: What are the best gloves for general building work?
faq.a: A nitrile- or PU-coated knitted glove with EN 388 abrasion level 3 or 4 covers most general site work — good grip, enough dexterity that it stays on, cheap enough to replace when torn. Move to a cut-rated version (level C+) when handling sheet metal, glass or blades.

Snug across the palm without pressure at the fingertips — measure around the knuckles and use the maker's size chart rather than guessing. Too big ruins grip and dexterity; too small fatigues the hand. Both end the same way: the glove comes off, and protection with it.

faq.q: When should work gloves be replaced?
faq.a: When the coating is holed or peeling, a seam splits, cut-resistant fibres are exposed, or the glove is soaked in oil that won't wash out. Damage removes the rated protection even if the glove still feels wearable — that's why site gloves are bought boxed.

pages.metaDesc: What the EN 388 marking on work gloves means — abrasion, cut, tear, puncture digits, the A–F ISO cut letter and P impact mark — with a live decoder for any marking.
pages.lede: Every rated work glove carries a shield with a string like 4X42F under it. Six positions, each one a lab test. Type yours into the decoder below — or read the whole system in the tables that follow.

blocks.html:
EN 388 covers gloves against mechanical risks. The marking under the shield reads left to right:

  • Digit 1 — abrasion (0–4): sandpaper cycles until the material wears through.
  • Digit 2 — cut, coup test (0–5): a rotating circular blade under fixed load.
  • Digit 3 — tear (0–4): force needed to rip the material.
  • Digit 4 — puncture (0–4): force to push a standard stylus through.
  • Letter 5 — cut, ISO 13997 "TDM" test (A–F): a straight blade under increasing load. Used because tough fibres blunt the coup test's blade — when that happens, this letter is the cut rating that counts and the coup digit shows X.
  • Letter 6 — P: passed the knuckle impact test (common on mechanics' and utilities gloves).

An X anywhere means "not tested" — not zero, but not proven either.

Type the marking printed under the EN 388 shield on your glove — like 4131, 4X42F or 3X43FP — and it translates position by position.

blocks.html: Why some gloves show X for cut but carry a letter: high-performance fibres blunt the coup test's rotating blade, making its result meaningless — so the standard requires the ISO 13997 test instead, the coup position is marked X, and the letter is the rating that counts. A glove marked 4X42F is a top-tier cut glove, not an untested one.

faq.q: What does 4131 mean on a glove?
faq.a: Reading the EN 388 digits: abrasion 4 (highest), cut 1 (light, coup test), tear 3 (good), puncture 1 (low). It's a classic general-handling grip glove — fine for materials and site work, wrong for real cut hazards.

faq.q: What does the X mean in an EN 388 rating?
faq.a: Not tested for that hazard. It isn't a zero and isn't a pass — the maker simply didn't run that test. On cut-resistant gloves an X in the coup position is normal: their fibres blunt that test's blade, so the ISO 13997 letter A–F is the valid cut rating.

faq.q: What cut level do I need for handling sheet metal?
faq.a: Cut level C (10 N on the ISO 13997 test) is the usual starting point for sheet metal and glazing, moving to D or above where edges are heavy, oily or handled at force. Specify by the letter, not the old coup digit.

faq.q: Is a higher EN 388 number always better?
faq.a: Higher means more protection in that one test, but protection trades against dexterity and comfort — and an over-specified glove that gets taken off protects nothing. Match each position to the actual hazard rather than buying the biggest numbers.
